source.version: arXiv preprint (PDF creator field 'arXiv GenPDF'); no version number or date printed on the document. It cites a New York Times article dated 2025-05-16 (p. 3, footnote 2), so this version postdates May 2025 even though the library file name says 2024.

paper_design_summary: A theory paper. The authors build a Bayesian model in which a continuum of users with heterogeneous preferences choose how much information to share with an AI, trading off output fidelity against communication cost. They prove and simulate that the population's output variance falls below the variance of preferences (homogenization), that training AI on AI output can cause a homogenization 'death spiral', and that AI bias can become societal bias. No human participants and no empirical data.

studies.label: Bayesian model of human-AI interaction with numerical simulations of a self-training loop

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; no participants. Model parameters (lambda, Gamma, prior distributions) are varied in proofs and simulations.
assignment.quote: we introduce a Bayesian framework in which heterogeneous users choose how much information to share with the AI, facing a trade-off between output fidelity and communication cost.

participants.who: No human participants. Users are a modeled continuum of types; simulations discretize the preference distribution (M = 1001 support points, T = 100 iterations).
participants.quote: there is a continuum of users of type θ ∈ Θ, denoting a user's specific preference about how to complete the task.
participants.locator: p. 8, Section 3; simulation settings p. e-17 (PDF p. 49-50), Appendix F

ai_tool.name_model: Abstract Bayesian AI that outputs its posterior mean; ChatGPT GPT-4o used only for an illustrative example (Figure 1)
ai_tool.how_used: Modeled: the user sends a costly noisy signal of her preference and the AI returns the posterior mean given its prior.

task.description: Generic task with a one-dimensional preference over outputs (examples: writing an abstract, a news article).

eligibility.reason: Theory paper (Bayesian model with proofs and numerical simulations). No human participants, no random assignment, and no output scored by raters or computed measures on real outputs. The codebook lists theory papers in the screening report and omits them from the dataset.

one_line_finding: In the model, when everyone uses AI the variance of population output is lower than the variance of preferences and falls as the cost of human-AI interaction rises (Theorem 1, p. 13; Figure 3, p. 14), and training AI on AI output can drive output variance toward zero (Figure 4, p. 16).
open_questions: design_class: the form has no 'theory' code. I used 'other'; 'model_only' is the alternative if that code is meant to cover all papers without human participants.
notes: Main text pp. 1-26, references, Appendix A (proofs), Online Supplement Appendices B-F (proofs, three-point distribution, simulation algorithms). The literature review (p. 5) cites Doshi and Hauser (2024), Wang et al. (2023), Anderson et al. (2024), and Padmakumar and He (2024) as empirical homogenization evidence; these may be candidates if not already screened. The 'simulations' are numerical solutions of the model, not experiments with people or LLMs.
